title: Words that connect the poems
scope: Patricia Smith, Blood Dazzler, pp. vii–24
intro: Select a word to compare its uses in the poems.
link_note: Lines show interpretive connections, not measured word co-occurrence.
count_note: Counts refer to exact words in poem bodies. Capitalization is ignored; related forms remain separate. Counts exclude titles and headnotes.

nodes.summary: Rain can be familiar and welcome before it becomes frightening. The same word carries the children’s play, an owner’s patience, and the storm’s change in scale.

examples.note: The homeowner waits patiently for rain beside the inherited house.
Children approach familiar rain; later mothers carry their lives to rooftops.

nodes.summary: Water sustains life and threatens it. A household leaves drinking water for its dog; floodwater later reaches people stranded on a roof.

examples.note: Luther B is left bowls of water while the household evacuates.
Water rises toward the feet of people waiting for rescue.

nodes.summary: Wind becomes a perceptible force: it acquires color in one poem and becomes a wall against Luther B’s body in another.

examples.note: Wind finds its color as the poem reconstructs the storm’s first sound.

examples.poem: Luther B Rides Out the Storm
examples.note: Luther B presses his muzzle against a wall of wind.

nodes.summary: A house can be the center of an inherited life or one property among several. The contrast changes what evacuation puts at risk.

examples.note: The speaker identifies the house with a grandfather, garden, food, and daily routine.
The affluent evacuee has a guest house, boat, car, and another home.

nodes.summary: Home promises a place to return to. That promise differs for the household leaving its dog and the evacuee able to exchange one home for another.

examples.note: The household promises to return home soon and retrieve Luther B.
The speaker treats evacuation as exchanging home for its vacation version.

nodes.summary: This possessive pronoun changes with its speaker. A resident claims the materials of a life; Katrina claims her appetite, name, and power.

examples.note: Repeated my ties the house, garden, table, dust, and food to the homeowner.
Katrina claims her mouth, name, fists, and swallowing eye.

nodes.summary: Money can give people more choices, but it cannot guarantee protection. Compare the affluent evacuation with the money-spell poem’s fragile defense against weather.

examples.note: Related contrast: dollar accompanies the car and vacation home; money itself does not occur here.
The poem describes money as too thin to hold tomorrow back.

nodes.summary: The same evacuation command reaches people with unequal resources. Its apparent simplicity conflicts with the practical work of leaving.

examples.note: A resident answers the television order by questioning transport and refuge.
The affluent speaker hears Go but can leave by car for another home.

nodes.summary: Leaving involves specific losses and decisions. The word directs people away from their belongings and directs a household to abandon its dog temporarily.

examples.note: The order lists a house, food, a dog, a watch, and a church hat.
The departing household says to leave Luther B behind.

nodes.summary: The command to run assumes movement is available. The wealthy evacuee has transport; the resident questions whether human bodies can meet the command.

examples.note: The television order says run; the resident questions its assumptions about bodies and transport.
The speaker says the household runs while describing departure in a Lincoln.

nodes.summary: Katrina’s storm eye becomes a hungry observer. Another speaker imagines people inside that eye, reversing the question from what the storm sees to whom it threatens.

examples.note: Katrina describes an eye that craves sights and pushes her forward.
The storm survivor describes a threatening woman with us in her eye.

nodes.summary: A mouth can consume or admit danger. Katrina fills hers with buildings; a survivor advises keeping a human mouth closed against the weather.

examples.note: Katrina says she has filled her mouth with buildings.
The survivor tells the listener to keep a mouth closed so weather cannot enter.

nodes.summary: Human bodies have limits that an evacuation instruction cannot remove. Their own water and protective bones become newly vulnerable as the storm arrives.

examples.note: The resident insists that bodies are only bodies, without wheels or gas.
The poem considers bodies already filled with water and secured by bone.

nodes.summary: Human eyes do not guarantee attention to human need. The television warning and the presidential performance expose different failures of recognition.

examples.note: The man’s gray eyes accompany a simple order; the resident questions whether he sees their limits.
The president’s dead eyes focus on the guitar chord while a woman voices abandonment.

nodes.summary: Seeing means appetite for Katrina and a demand for recognition for the resident. Compare what each observer notices and what each overlooks.

examples.note: Katrina wants to see even the sound of weeping.
The resident asks whether the television man can see the limits of their bodies.

nodes.summary: Sound crosses into sight and color. These impossible sensory combinations give the storm a presence that ordinary observation cannot contain.

examples.note: Katrina’s eye wants to see the sound of weeping.
The storm’s first sound is repeatedly described as purple.

nodes.summary: Purple connects a familiar possession with an unfamiliar sensory event. The color moves from a church hat to the storm’s sound and wounded imagery.

examples.note: A purple church hat belongs to the life the resident is told to leave.
Purple describes the first sound through the image of a new wound.

nodes.summary: A name can confer identity or authority. Katrina’s naming gives her force; the preacher’s claimed familiarity with Jesus supports his standing among the congregation.

examples.note: Receiving a name gives Katrina pulse, temper, and a word in her own mouth.
The congregation credits the preacher with knowing Jesus by his first name.

nodes.summary: Knowing can mean familiarity with home or recognition of a threat. Katrina demands recognition; residents describe what makes an unfamiliar destination difficult to imagine.

examples.note: The resident says bodies remain tied to what they know.
Katrina warns people that they must not know her name.

nodes.summary: God is invoked as commanding authority and as the destination of desperate protest. Religious language does not establish that protection arrives.

examples.note: The television order is compared with God directing people out of Paradise.
The roof survivor directs angry cries toward God while holding babies.

nodes.summary: The person being addressed changes. The prologue places you with a visitor drawn to the city; the roof poem places you inside exposure, judgment, and uncertain rescue.

examples.poem: Prologue: And Then She Owns You
examples.note: A visitor is addressed as someone attracted and held by New Orleans.
The addressed person signals from a roof, holds babies, and faces rescue decisions.

links.note: Leaving a structure also puts inherited routines, food, and belongings at risk. Compare pp. 7–8.
The same command meets unequal means of escape: compare the resident on p. 7 with the car and second home on p. 13.
Water is already inside human bodies, yet floodwater threatens their protection. Compare pp. 19–20 with p. 23.
Katrina’s hungry eye contrasts with the attention of human authorities. Compare p. 4 with the television man on p. 7 and president on p. 22.
The resident’s possessive claims preserve a life; Katrina’s claims announce an appetite for buildings. Compare pp. 8 and 11.
The resident asks for recognition of familiar attachments and bodily limits. Read the uses of know and see together on p. 7.
The roof poem connects direct address with rising water, making the survivor’s exposure the reader’s immediate point of view. Read p. 23.

evidence_note: Each example is a paraphrase. The money example on p. 13 is explicitly a related contrast using dollar, not another occurrence of money. Eye and eyes are separate exact words; the television man’s eyes are gray, not described as white.
source_note: Reading: Patricia Smith, Blood Dazzler (Coffee House Press, 2008), pp. vii–24. All page references use the book’s printed pages.
